output:
Sunlight looks white, but it is really a mixture of every colour. Red, orange, yellow, green, blue and violet all travel together in one beam. Each colour moves as a wave, and the waves differ in length. Red waves are long and lazy. Blue and violet waves are short and tight.

When sunlight enters the atmosphere, it meets countless molecules of nitrogen and oxygen. These are far smaller than the waves passing through them. Short waves bump into these molecules and get flung off in all directions. Long waves mostly sail straight past, barely disturbed.

So blue light gets scattered across the whole sky, arriving at your eyes from every direction at once. That is why the dome above you glows blue rather than looking black.

Picture throwing tennis balls and beach balls at a forest of thin poles. The small balls ricochet everywhere, while the big ones slip between the gaps.

Violet scatters even more than blue, but your eyes are less sensitive to it, and some is absorbed higher up. Blue wins out.

At sunset, light travels through much more air to reach you. The blue is scattered away entirely, leaving the reds and oranges behind.

In short, the sky is blue because air scatters short blue waves in every direction.
